catalog_quote: Stress in Taruma is not lexical, but usually fixed on the penultimate syllable (27a-d). Words ending in -n have final stress (27e-f). Monosyllabic words are always stressed (27g). ... Exceptions to this pattern include words with ante-penultimate stress, namely kiribi ['kje.ɾe.be] ‘mix’ and dja’obarada [dʑa.ʔo.'ba.ɾa.da] ‘four’, as well as words with word-final stress, namely akoka [a.ko.'ka] ‘you’, ikya [i.'kjia] ‘3’, makoki [ma.ko.'kji] ‘go’ and any verb ending the suffix -hĩ, such as chokohĩ [tɕo.ko.'hĩ] ‘tell’. It is not apparent at this point what causes these exceptions. ... When suffixes attach to nouns, stress is often reassigned so that it remains penultimate. ... To sum up, stress is usually penultimate in uninflected roots and is often reassigned to penultimate syllable when nouns are inflected with -ki, -kwa, and -ka. With -ni, stress is only reassigned in disyllabic words, and with -ma it is only reassigned in disyllabic words where the second syllable is heavier than the first. In verbs, word-final stress signals the imperative. It should be noted, however, that the suffixes -ma and -ka appear more frequently in the data than the others, so that the stress patterns described here can be subject to change as more data emerges.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; words ending in -n take final stress; monosyllables are stressed. Under suffixation stress is often re-assigned so that it stays penultimate (always with -kwa 'LOC' and -ki 'INS'; with -ni only in disyllabic roots; with -ma only when the root's second syllable is heavier than the first; with -ka depending on root syllable count), and word-final stress marks the imperative in verbs (p. 41-42). Phonetically stress = higher pitch and greater loudness, with shortening of unstressed vowels (p. 39).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions with antepenultimate stress (kiribi 'mix', dja'obarada 'four') and with final stress (akoka 'you', ikya '3', makoki 'go'); all verbs ending in the suffix -hĩ have final stress; words in final -n have final stress; imperative verbs shift stress to the last syllable; some suffixed nouns keep root stress (antepenultimate) rather than re-assigning (e.g. karikari-ka, hichi-ka, adama). Author notes the pattern may change as more data emerge (p. 42).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in elicited words and short utterances from the last three (elderly) speakers in Turunau/Maruranau, Guyana, recorded remotely by in-situ community researchers in 2020-2021 plus Meira's 2015 recordings; §3.4.2 treats utterance-level intonation separately (falling final pitch in declaratives, rising in interrogatives).
new_statements.identity_note: Same variety as Glottolog taru1236 (Taruma, isolate, ISO tdm). Data are from the last three speakers in Turunau (part of Maruranau village, South Rupununi, Guyana), who are Wapishana-dominant; Serke notes heavy Wapishana/Waiwai contact influence but treats the language as Taruma proper. No dialect division is described.

new_statements.quote: The Taruma phoneme inventory consists of 20 consonant and 8 vowel phonemes. The principal phonological processes include the palatalization of most consonants before /i/ and the lenition of /p/ before /o/. Taruma is non-tonal, and stress is generally penultimate.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate; penultimate stress) and as the existing Serke 2022 statement (penultimate, non-lexical). Adds the explicit 'non-tonal' classification. It is a one-line summary by the same team (Serke and Rybka are co-authors) rather than an independent analysis, so it does not add weight-sensitivity, secondary stress or exception detail beyond Serke 2022.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is normally on the penultimate syllable; the language has no tone. 'Generally' signals exceptions but the appendix does not list them.
new_statements.exceptions: None specified beyond the hedge 'generally penultimate'. (Serke 2022, the phonology this appendix summarises, gives the exceptions: final stress in words ending in -n, antepenultimate stress in a few words such as kiribi and dja'ob.)
new_statements.identity_note: The 2024 article documents the Taruma of the Maroranaawa Wapichan community, South Rupununi, Guyana (speakers Irene and Vincent Louis, siblings); the language is described as having only about three speakers. This is the same variety and the same speakers as Serke 2022. No dialect differentiation is described.
